claude.sample_unit: junior physicians (27 patient images each, 540 descriptions)

links.outcome: HPO description accuracy of physicians with vs without MLLM assistance, plus standalone MLLM accuracy
links.quote: Of the 270 descriptions collected from each group, the MLLM-assisted group achieved a correctness rate of 67.4% (182/270), while the manual group achieved 20.4% (55/270).

links.outcome: Clinician performance with AI in workflow versus without AI and versus standalone model
links.effect: Physician+ChatGPT-4o accuracy 67.4% exceeded standalone ChatGPT-4o (48%) and manual searching (20.4%).
links.quote: Our study reveals that collaboration between junior physicians and ChatGPT-4o significantly enhances HPO description accuracy for rare diseases, outperforming both traditional methods and standalone MLLM use.

links.outcome: Whether physicians detected or were misled by incorrect AI outputs (anchoring)
links.effect: For Bardet-Biedl syndrome, MLLM missed 'polydactyly'; error rate was higher in MLLM-assisted group (6/10) than manual (4/10), though overall accuracy improved.
links.quote: This led to a higher error rate in the MLLM-assisted group (6/10 physicians) compared to the manual group (4/10).

links.outcome: Fabricated or mismatched HPO terms and IDs generated by MLLMs
links.effect: Incorrect IDs: ChatGPT-4o 57.3% (67/117), Llama3.2:11b 98% (62/63), Llama3.2:90b 82% (46/56); fabricated terms 34.2%, 41%, 32%.
links.quote: Verification revealed that 57.3% (67/117) had incorrect IDs, and 34.2% (40/117) were fabricated, as they could not be retrieved on the HPO website.

links.outcome: Hallucinated HPO terms and IDs in AI outputs requiring verification
links.effect: High hallucination rates across three MLLMs (incorrect IDs 57-98%, fabricated terms 32-41%), so outputs need verification against the HPO database.
links.quote: Finally, for academic discourse or use in phenotype-driven diagnostic tools, generated HPO terms should be validated against the HPO database to ensure accuracy.

unlisted_practices: Using an MLLM to pre-identify standardized ontology terms as prompts to support junior physicians' phenotype coding in rare disease

links.quote: Of the 270 descriptions collected from each group, the MLLM-assisted group achieved a correctness rate of 67.4% (182/270), while the manual group achieved 20.4% (55/270).
Among the 27 patient images, ChatGPT-4o achieved an accuracy rate of 48% (13/27), while Llama3.2:11b and Llama3.2:90b achieved rates of 15% (4/27) and 18% (5/27), respectively ( Table 3 ).

Specifically, ChatGPT-4o, Llama3.2:11b, and Llama3.2:90b generated incorrect IDs in 57.3% (67/117), 98% (62/63), and 82% (46/56) of cases, respectively, and fabricated terms in 34.2% (40/117), 41% (26/63), and 32% (18/56) of cases, respectively.

links.outcome: Errors after an incorrect model suggestion
links.effect: Bardet-Biedl error rate was 6/10 MLLM-assisted physicians vs 4/10 manual physicians.
links.quote: This led to a higher error rate in the MLLM-assisted group (6/10 physicians) compared to the manual group (4/10).

screen.practice: clinician verification of MLLM-suggested HPO terms via database search
screen.reason: The study empirically tests whether providing clinicians with MLLM-preidentified HPO terms improves phenotypic diagnostic accuracy compared to manual standard practice, while also evaluating hallucination rates.

primary.practice: AI-assisted clinical workflow vs manual search
